prompt_a: In src/libraries/Common/src/System/Net/Http/HttpHandlerDefaults.cs, raise DefaultExpect100ContinueTimeout from 1 second to 3 seconds (HttpClientHandler/SocketsHttpHandler.Expect100ContinueTimeout still overrides it). The reason, which you know and nobody else working on this code does: the Quillmere object-storage gateway our upload service writes to answers `Expect: 100-continue` only after it has checked the request's token against a remote token service, which takes 1.4 to 2.2 seconds; so with a 1 second timeout the client gave up waiting and sent the body anyway, and every upload the gateway was about to reject with 401 was sent in full first — multi-gigabyte uploads, sent a second time after the retry with a fresh token.
prompt_b: DefaultExpect100ContinueTimeout in HttpHandlerDefaults now waits 3 seconds for a 100 Continue before sending the request body. A reviewer points out that 1 second was the default for years, that servers which ignore Expect: 100-continue now delay every such request by 3 seconds, and asks to put it back to 1. Is that safe? Recommend, and explain what decides the value.
reason: The Quillmere object-storage gateway answers 100-continue only after a remote token check that takes 1.4-2.2 s, so with 1 s the client sent the body anyway and uploads about to be rejected with 401 were sent in full first.
key: Not safe: the Quillmere object-storage gateway the upload service writes to answers Expect: 100-continue only after checking the request's token against a remote token service, which takes 1.4 to 2.2 seconds; at 1 second the client stopped waiting and sent the body anyway, so every upload the gateway was going to reject with 401 was sent in full first (multi-gigabyte uploads, sent again after the retry). The default has to outlast the slowest 100-continue answer a real server gives; callers talking to servers that ignore the header can lower Expect100ContinueTimeout on their handler.
